doc.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: No regrets; born in Attleboro and early musical exposure
summary: Conniff says he is fortunate to have done what he loves, was born in Attleboro in 1916, and was exposed to music by his parents; his dad taught him trombone at about nine.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: [coughs] pardon me. I hope there won’t be too much of that going on. I’ve got one of these California flu bugs or something. Oh, sure, you know, as we live life at the time, when we’re doing, like now what we’re doing, we think we’re doing the right thing for now. And I guess if you went back and looked at every now, you thought you were doing — I can see times when I probably could have done something a little differently, but I think on the whole, yeah, I’ve been very fortunate. Well the main thing I guess I’ve been fortunate about is that there aren’t a lot of men probably that go through a lifetime and do what they really love to do. You know and I have had that happen to me in this life, and I’m very grateful for that, yeah. You mentioned the 50s, and your family, and playing Ray Conniff, and I was born in Attleboro, Massachusetts in 1916, and I would say I was

exposed to music, you know, from my mom and dad as a child. And see I have recollections of five and six you know, musical recollections. And so what are we talking about? Well ‘56 I did my first album, for Columbia Records. So we’re talking about 40 years, right in the middle of the whole thing, when you started hearing it. People thought in 1956, when my first album came out, like they think about everybody that becomes popular. “Wow, overnight guy here, where’s he been?” But as you think about it there have been 40 years of exposure to music, and my dad played piano, a little piano — he used to play mostly ump-chink chords and sing me little humorous songs you know, and that tickled the heck out of me. But, those little ump-chink chords instilled a rhythm into me, and made me very conscious of rhythm. And then he also played trombone. When I got a little older he taught me to play the trombone when I was about nine. And my mom played piano and used to sing songs to me. So I was exposed to music. I’m 81 now, so I was exposed to music about 40 years when you first heard about me.
